Computational expense has been an obstacle to this type of discovery approach to photochemistry, especially in cases where modeling of subsequent reactions on the “hot” ground state is required. The few cases where this has been previously possible are restricted to very small molecules and/or very small barrier reactions (occurring within less than a picosecond) on the ground state.46-48 In order to describe the topology of conical intersections correctly and avoid intrinsic convergence 3 LLNL-JRNL-822958 difficulties near these intersections, we use multireference wavefunction methods and eschew the problematic time-dependent density functional theory methods.49,50 Ab initio Multiple Spawning (AIMS)51-54 coupled to TeraChem55-57 was used to describe the initial photoisomerization. Trajectory basis functions (TBFs) are spawned on the ground state to describe electronic transitions mediated by conical intersections. Once the ground-excited state energy gap becomes large, it becomes very unlikely that further electronic state transitions will occur. With this procedure, we identified critical intermediates that are involved in the open-to-close transformation and several competing pathways, shedding light on key elements for future design strategies. The DASA switching mechanism is initiated by the absorption of 545nm light, promoting the open-form (A, Figure 2), initially in the EEZZ configuration (E/Z labels refer to the E/Z configuration assumed by the , , ,  bonds, respectively), to an electronically excited state via a * transition (molecular orbitals involved in the transition are shown in Figure S1). In our recent theoretical stuudy,58 we showed that A primarily relaxes back to the ground state forming A' (EEEZ) through a Z/E photoisomerization consisting of a one-bond flip around the C -C double 3 4 bond ( in Figure 2). During the internal conversion through the conical intersection, the incident photon’s energy is transformed into nuclear kinetic energy which at short timescales (before internal vibrational energy redistribution) is concentrated in a few vibrational modes along the backbone of A'. Consequently, the molecule explores several configurations and reaction pathways that could be inaccessible in an equilibrium regime. In addition to the productive pathway along , Figure 2 shows several competing channels are possible upon nonradiative decay to the ground- state due to isomerization around alternate dihedral angles of the hexatriene bridge. In the following, we quantify our findings by following the wavepacket dynamics during the course of the discovery-based ground-state dynamics. In Figure 3, we show how the energy absorbed via the incident photon manifests in nuclear motion highlighting the time-evolution of the crucial intermediates along the discovered pathways in Figure 2.
